verdict.reason: Skip it; the premise collapses under its own weight and there's no evidence the execution justifies the theatrical trip. A teenager hearing a voice and training for a marathon is a thin high-concept gimmick, not a story, and nothing in the film's pedigree or venue suggests Johnny Meier has found the emotional or musical substance to make it work.

ratings.plot: The higher self calls through leaf and bird, awakening what has always lived within.

verdict.reason: A short film about spiritual awakening plays better as a streaming discovery than as a theater trip. Without runtime, format details, or venue distinction, there's no reason to leave home for this.

ratings.plot: A filmmaker applies lessons from a Hallmark movie writing workshop to pitch a documentary about concrete.

verdict.reason: John Wilson's deadpan absurdism works best as a complete experience, but a 100-minute film about pitching a concrete doc tests patience even for his fans. The IFC Center screening matters here—this is Wilson's home venue, and the crowd will be primed for his particular brand of humor.

movies.title: HEARTS OF DARKNESS: A FILMMAKER’S APOCALYPSE

ratings.plot: Three friends in their mid-thirties as they road trip across the Midwestern United States in search of their friend who has seemingly disappeared off the grid.

verdict.reason: Shatara Michelle Ford's debut feature has real emotional depth, but two hours of Midwestern driving and interpersonal tension works better in a living room than a theater seat. The intimate ensemble drama and conversational pacing reward attention but don't demand the big screen.

ratings.plot: A washed-up New York party promoter is forced to turn his life around when an unexpected visitor arrives.

verdict.reason: Jordan Firstman's directorial debut has uneven execution that doesn't justify the 126-minute runtime, despite moments of genuine comic insight. The film works better as a character study than as a structured narrative, making it worth catching at home rather than committing a full evening to it at Lincoln Center.

ratings.plot: Follows a mother, her daughter, and a teenage boy blamed for a tragic death as they travel to Tenerife together, confronting grief, blame, and forgiveness on a family holiday that never happened.

verdict.reason: Wollner's new work has real depth, but two hours of grief excavation on a fabricated holiday tests patience without payoff. The Lincoln Center screening matters only if you're tracking her direction after *The Trouble with Being Born*.

ratings.plot: Rose, a German widow, hides from Russian soldiers who like to rape women and fights off Polish refugees who will steal everything she has. She gets help when Tadeusz, a former Polish officer, arrives looking to hide from his past.
A portrait of genius music composer Ryuichi Sakamoto.
In 1951, a group of high schoolers come of age in a bleak, isolated, atrophied North Texas town that is slowly dying, both culturally and economically.

Friends on a late-night food run become trapped on an infinite highway with otherworldly terrors lurking beyond. Confined in their Jeep Cherokee, they must decide whether to accept their fate or attempt escape.

verdict.reason: A high-concept trap film that works best as a midnight screening experience, but the 89-minute runtime and confined setting limit its theatrical pull. The gimmick—an infinite highway and a Jeep—is visual enough for the big screen, but only if you're ready for claustrophobic genre work.

movies.title: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows – Part 2

ratings.plot: Harry, Ron and Hermione set out on a quest to eliminate the remaining horcruxes. On the other hand, the students and teachers must unite to defend Hogwarts against Lord Voldemort and his army.

verdict.reason: The finale delivers on spectacle and closure, but it's a 13-year-old film playing standard formats at multiplexes where it's been available for years. Watch it if you want to see the battle of Hogwarts on a big screen tonight; otherwise, this one works just fine at home.

ratings.plot: In the wake of his mother's death and his father's remarriage, a headstrong boy ventures into a dreamlike world shared by the living and the dead in search of his missing stepmother.
When a cartoon rabbit is accused of murder, he enlists the help of a burnt out private investigator to prove his innocence.

Two kids become spies in attempt to save their ex-spies parents from an evil mastermind. Armed with a bag of high tech gadgets, Carmen and Juni will bravely crisscross the globe on a mission to save their parents and maybe even th...

verdict.reason: Rodriguez's visual playfulness and practical invention are worth a theater, but the script aims low and the novelty has worn thin since 2001. The Alamo crowd will have fun; everyone else can skip it.

A holiday film at Lincoln Center worth catching if you're already in the neighborhood, but not essential viewing. The runtime and theatrical appeal remain unclear without more information about the film itself.

ratings.plot: Amziah King, beekeeper, musician, and anchor of his community, reunites with former foster daughter Kateri after many years apart, and fends off threats to his honey business.

verdict.reason: Andrew Patterson has earned attention for sharp filmmaking, but 130 minutes testing a premise built on beekeeping and community tension risks overstaying its welcome. The Village East screening offers no special format or restoration to justify the runtime commitment.

movies.title: Harry Potter & the Goblet of Fire

ratings.plot: Harry Potter finds himself competing in a hazardous tournament between rival schools of magic, but he is distracted by recurring nightmares.

verdict.reason: The turning point where the series darkens works best on a big screen, but the 157-minute runtime and uneven pacing test patience on a weeknight. Mike Newell's direction prioritizes spectacle over character, so unless you're revisiting the theatrical experience or catching it in 4DX, streaming is the smarter choice.

ratings.plot: When a lovesick musician is given the wrong number for his dream girl, he teams up with a driven psychology student to find her. Together, they spark a hilarious campus-wide frenzy that tests their own hearts and ambitions along t...

verdict.reason: Light romantic comedy with enough charm to work as a night out, but nothing here demands the big screen over streaming in a few months. Alicia MacDonald keeps the pacing brisk and the ensemble cast commits to the bit, which matters more than the premise.

ratings.plot: A food influencer secretly struggles with bulimia as she navigates online fame, close friendships, and a painful past.
A couple lose their home and later discover the husband has been diagnosed with a terminal illness as they embark on a year long coastal trek.

verdict.reason: Marianne Elliott's film has real emotional weight but falters in execution, landing somewhere between TV drama and theatrical cinema. The two leads carry the weight, but the runtime asks more of the material than it can sustain.

movies.title: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince

ratings.plot: As Harry Potter begins his sixth year at Hogwarts, he discovers an old book marked as "the property of the Half-Blood Prince" and begins to learn more about Lord Voldemort's dark past.

verdict.reason: A solid middle chapter that works better on rewatch than opening night, but 4DX adds nothing to a character-driven film that needs breathing room. The 153-minute runtime plays heavy, and the theatrical experience doesn't justify the subway trip over a home viewing.

ratings.plot: A somewhat prim and proper Englishman is hired as the tutor to the son of the Japanese ambassador. His life changes when he and the boy are kidnapped by terrorists for political purposes.

verdict.reason: A forgotten 1975 adventure with real craft, but the 99-minute runtime and dated action sequences demand patience for a film better suited to home viewing. Lincoln Center's repertory programming gives it theatrical legitimacy, though this is a deep-catalog recovery rather than an essential rediscovery.

ratings.plot: A homesick, no-nonsense lounge singer decides to leave New York City to spend some time visiting her two sisters and brother on the West Coast. Eventually she falls in love with a down-and-out ex-jazz pianist.

verdict.reason: Walsh's melodrama has strong atmosphere but lacks the punch of his best work. Lupino's performance elevates material that never quite catches fire.

movies.title: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets

ratings.plot: Harry Potter lives his second year at Hogwarts with Ron and Hermione when a message on the wall announces that the legendary Chamber of Secrets has been opened. The trio soon realize that, to save the school, it will take a lot of...

verdict.reason: Skip the theatrical re-release unless you need the big-screen nostalgia hit, since this film lands safely but without distinction on a second viewing at home. Columbus shoots it competently but the 161-minute runtime punishes patience for a story that works better compressed.

ratings.plot: Professor Se Jeong attends a biotech conference, only to witness it spiral into catastrophe when a rapidly mutating virus is unleashed. As the outbreak spreads and the infected begin to transform, authorities seal off the entire f...

verdict.reason: Yeon Sang-ho knows how to stage action set pieces, and this virus-outbreak thriller has enough kinetic energy to justify a theater trip if you're in the mood for spectacle over story. The 122-minute runtime asks patience for a premise that's been done better, and the gap between the director's ambitions and the execution keeps this from being essential.

ratings.plot: After Clive Randolph finally returns home from Gold Coast colony, younger brother John balks at following the family Colonial Service tradition. But back in Gold Coast, one Zurof, nominally studying ants, pursues a hidden politica...

verdict.reason: A spirited 1939 imperial adventure with real craft, but the colonial politics feel quaint now and the runtime tests patience. See it at IFC if you're committed to pre-war Hollywood spectacle, otherwise wait for home viewing.

ratings.plot: In 1940, Henri Marre arrives in Vichy with his self-taught political manuscript Notre Salut, hoping to establish himself in the new regime and publish his work. He seeks to save France from collapse—or perhaps himself.

verdict.reason: A serious period film about collaboration and ambition in Vichy France has real substance, but the 155-minute runtime demands commitment to a morally murky protagonist with no clear dramatic payoff. Emmanuel Marre's directorial voice matters more than the material itself, and Lincoln Center is the right venue if you're in the mood for slow, uncompromising European cinema.

ratings.plot: Macbeth, the Thane of Glamis, receives a prophecy from a trio of witches that one day he will become King of Scotland. Consumed by ambition and spurred to action by his wife, Macbeth murders his king and takes the throne for himself.

verdict.reason: Kurzel's 2015 version is visually striking and brutal, but Shakespeare's language and a relatively young Michael Fassbender sometimes strain against the muddy, visceral approach. Watch for ambition; skip if you want the play to breathe.

ratings.plot: A modern family relocates to the countryside where the children discover a magical tree with eccentric residents. They're transported to fantastical lands, rekindling their family bond through adventures.

verdict.reason: Skip this if you need an adventure that earns its runtime; 110 minutes is too long for a children's film with this premise. The film works best as a casual family outing on a lazy afternoon, not a theatrical event worth the subway ride.

movies.title: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix

ratings.plot: With their warning about Lord Voldemort's return scoffed at, Harry and Dumbledore are targeted by the Wizard authorities as an authoritarian bureaucrat slowly seizes power at Hogwarts.

verdict.reason: Skip the 4DX gimmick and catch this on a regular screen if you want to revisit Yates' tightest Potter film. The Ministry subplot works better than the bloat that comes later, but 138 minutes still drags in the middle act.

ratings.plot: A mysterious discovery is made on the outskirts of the remote harbor town. The residents find themselves in a desperate fight for survival against something they have never encountered before.

verdict.reason: Na Hong-jin brings real formal control to genre material, but 160 minutes of survival horror tests patience even when the execution is solid. The HDR screening at Downtown Brooklyn is the only reason to catch this in theaters rather than wait for home viewing.

ratings.plot: A criminal psychologist who turned agoraphobic after a murder attempt agrees to help two San Francisco detectives hunt for a copycat serial killer who intends on making her his next victim.

verdict.reason: A sharp 90s thriller with real tension between Sigourney Weaver's agoraphobic psychologist and the serial killer hunting her, but the runtime drags and the third act relies on plot mechanics rather than character. The theatrical experience matters here—Weaver's claustrophobia plays better on a big screen than at home.

ratings.plot: An intellectually nonconformist friar investigates a series of mysterious deaths in an isolated abbey.

verdict.reason: Annaud's adaptation is handsome and absorbing for two hours, but it flattens Umberto Eco's Byzantine theology into a whodunit that feels safer on home video. The 130-minute runtime tests patience by the final act.

ratings.plot: Scottish warrior William Wallace leads his countrymen in a rebellion to free his homeland from the tyranny of King Edward I of England.

verdict.reason: Gibson's direction is uneven and the historical liberties are substantial, but the scale and passion of the battle sequences remain potent on a large screen. The 178-minute runtime demands commitment, and this works better as a theatrical event than a home viewing.

ratings.plot: Two rock-bottom drivers transport a wealthy teen to rehab, but their simple job spirals into a chaotic journey of drugs, danger, and crime as their passenger derails their plans.

verdict.reason: Macon Blair has an ear for character chaos and dark comedy, but the film's uneven execution and thin premise suggest it works better as a rental than a theater commitment. The 98-minute runtime keeps things brisk, so if you're in the mood for a low-stakes crime caper with laughs, the Alamo Drafthouse locations offer the right vibe.

ratings.plot: A young beautician, newly arrived in a small Louisiana town, finds work at the local salon, where a small group of women share a close bond of friendship, and welcome her into the fold.

verdict.reason: A solid ensemble drama with genuine warmth, but the theatrical re-release offers nothing new over the home version. The film plays best in small doses on a living room TV, not as a full two-hour commitment in a multiplex.

ratings.plot: In a French seaside town, at a boarding house for civil servants recovering from surgery and maladies, the six male residents' lives change dramatically when two women arrive: Catherine, lively, sexually liberated, willing to kiss...

verdict.reason: Jacques Brel's only narrative film is a curiosity worth exploring if you're at Lincoln Center, but the 91 minutes meander through bedroom comedy that hasn't aged as freely as it imagined. The sexual liberation angle plays quaint now, and Brel's direction lacks the bite his songs carried.

ratings.plot: A young man struggles with his desire to study art when his family thinks he's headed for premedical studies. Conflicts between Filipino traditions and expectations vs. personal dreams in the contemporary world erupt at his sister...

verdict.reason: A sharp-eyed debut about generational collision in a Filipino-American family that works best if you're in the mood for intimate character drama over plot momentum. The 88-minute runtime and ensemble cast keep things moving, but this is a film that rewards patience with specificity rather than broad appeal.

ratings.plot: The life and death of "Dracula" writer Bram Stoker is discussed, as well as the themes of the novel and several film adaptations of "Dracula," and the cultural impact of the work. While critics of the time were not receptive to th...

verdict.reason: A slim documentary about a canonical novel and its afterlife has real value, but the 56-minute runtime feels slight for a theater trip. Film Forum's 35mm print offers the best argument to go—that format choice matters when the alternative is streaming.

ratings.plot: In May of 2020, a standoff between a small-town sheriff and mayor sparks a powder keg as neighbor is pitted against neighbor in Eddington, New Mexico.

verdict.reason: Aster's tonal ambition is visible but the execution stumbles across 148 minutes, and this dark comedy-western hybrid works better in theory than in practice. Metrograph's DCP presentation is the right venue if you're willing to commit to an uneven swing at genre collision.

ratings.plot: A chronicle of the tragic love affair between American poet Elizabeth Bishop and Brazilian architect Lota de Macedo Soares.

verdict.reason: This is worth seeing if you're drawn to the specificity of Bishop and Lota's relationship, but the film doesn't quite justify its two-hour runtime. Barreto's direction is workmanlike rather than revelatory, and the emotional stakes flatten before the end.

ratings.plot: Grossly overweight yet good-hearted professor Sherman Klump takes a special chemical that turns him into the slim but obnoxious Buddy Love.

verdict.reason: Eddie Murphy's dual performance carries a middling comedy that works best as comfort viewing rather than a theater event. The 95-minute runtime and broad slapstick hold up better on a couch than in a packed multiplex.

ratings.plot: The hit musical based on the life of Eva Perón (Evita Duarte), a B-picture Argentinian actress who eventually became the wife of Argentinian president Juan Domingo Perón, and the most beloved and hated woman in Argentina.

verdict.reason: Parker's musical is uneven and bloated, but Metrograph's 35mm print restores the Dariush Wolcott cinematography to theatrical grandeur. See it only if you want the image, not the film.

ratings.plot: The Autobots must stop a colossal planet-consuming robot who goes after the Autobot Matrix of Leadership. At the same time, they must defend themselves against an all-out attack from the Decepticons.

verdict.reason: Skip unless you're seeing it at Alamo Drafthouse for the theatrical experience and nostalgia factor. The 1986 animated film is a cult object that plays better as a communal event than alone, and at 84 minutes it's slight enough for a night out without demanding much.

ratings.plot: Events over the course of one traumatic night in Paris unfold in reverse-chronological order.

verdict.reason: Only worth the trip if you can handle Noé's most punishing work without walking out. The reverse chronology structure and 13-minute single-take rape scene make this an endurance test that demands big-screen commitment.

ratings.plot: A police lieutenant uncovers more than he bargained for as his investigation of a series of murders, which have all the hallmarks of the deceased Gemini serial killer, leads him to question the patients of a psychiatric ward.

verdict.reason: Blatty's directorial vision has moments of genuine unease that justify the runtime, but the film sprawls and loses focus in ways that make it better suited to home viewing. The famous decapitation scene remains a knockout, but it cannot carry two hours of narrative confusion.

ratings.plot: A grieving father enacts his long-awaited revenge against a ruthless gang on Christmas Eve.

verdict.reason: John Woo's first English-language film in years has genuine craft moments, but the execution is uneven and the premise wears thin before the final act. The Lincoln Center booking is respectable, but this is a minor entry from a major director—worth catching only if you're committed to tracking his recent work.

ratings.plot: Jim Morrison's life, from his LA film student days to his death in Paris. Val Kilmer delivers an uncanny portrayal, with vocals indistinguishable from Morrison's originals. It depicts Morrison's journey as the iconic 60s rock fron...

verdict.reason: Val Kilmer's vocal mimicry is genuinely uncanny and worth hearing in a theater, but Stone's approach is more fever dream than biography, so manage expectations for narrative coherence. The 140-minute runtime asks a lot for a film that often prioritizes spectacle over insight.

ratings.plot: A violent police detective investigates a brutal murder that might involve a manipulative and seductive novelist.

verdict.reason: Verhoeven's 1992 pulp is sleek, nasty, and fun in ways that feel genuinely transgressive, but it's also hollow beneath the surface seduction. The Alamo screenings honor its B-movie ambitions if you're in the mood for camp with edge.

ratings.plot: An adaptation of Homer's great epic, the film follows the assault on Troy by the united Greek forces.

verdict.reason: Skip the theatrical experience unless you're committed to seeing a baggy, uneven epic on 35mm film at Metrograph. The 163-minute runtime and narrative sprawl work better compressed at home, but the restoration print is worth the trip if you're already downtown and have the time.

movies.title: The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas

ratings.plot: A town's Sheriff and regular patron of a historical whorehouse fights to keep it running when a television reporter targets it as the Devil's playhouse.
After her mother commits suicide, a young woman travels to Italy in search of love, truth and a deeper connection with herself.

verdict.reason: Bertolucci's uneven chamber piece has genuine moments of visual grace, but the film's reach exceeds its grasp and the pacing sags in its second half. Metrograph is showing it on 35mm, which makes the Tuscan light worth seeing large, though streaming at home won't hurt you.

ratings.plot: In April 1964, more than twenty years after the Nazis won World War II, S.S. officer Xavier March uncovers a plot to eliminate the attendees of the Wannsee Conference so that Germany can establish better relations with the U.S.

verdict.reason: A fumbled alternate-history thriller that wastes its premise, but the 1994 HBO production has enough production design and Rutger Hauer's weary performance to justify a single viewing at Lincoln Center if you're committed to exploring '90s speculative television. The film's earnest mid-budget craft—swallowing the clumsy narrative—holds up better on a theater screen than it would on a small one.

ratings.plot: A classic tale about bitter relationships between a frivolous girl and a soldier is adapted for the post-World War II time.

verdict.reason: Clouzot's adaptation has genuine power but arrives uneven and padded at 100 minutes. The Film at Lincoln Center restoration makes this the only way to see it properly on a big screen, and the post-war Paris setting carries real historical weight if you're willing to sit with the film's tonal shifts.

ratings.plot: The wife of a university research scientist believes that her lakeside Vermont home is haunted by a ghost - or that she is losing her mind.

verdict.reason: Zemeckis's craft elevates a thin supernatural mystery into something watchable, but the 130-minute runtime drags a third-act twist that doesn't earn its setup. The 35mm print at Metrograph is the only reason to see it in a theater instead of streaming.

ratings.plot: Three actors accept an invitation to a Mexican village to perform their onscreen bandit fighter roles, unaware that it is the real thing.
Grieving hairdresser Justice goes on a road trip from South Central L.A. to Oakland on a mail truck alongside her friend and an obnoxious postal worker.

Apartment building superintendent Cleveland Heep rescues what he thinks is a young woman from the pool he maintains. When he discovers that she is actually a character from a bedtime story who is trying to make the journey back to...

verdict.reason: Shyamalan's strangest work has cult defenders, and the 35mm print at Metrograph makes it worth seeing if you're game for failure dressed up as ambition. The theatrical experience rescues nothing, but the film's delusional conviction about its own mythology is at least committed enough to deserve a big screen.

movies.title: A Day in the Country + People on Sunday

ratings.plot: American Job is a narrative film about Randy Scott, a youth caught in the dismal confusion of living and working in the world of minimum wage. American Job follows main character Randy Scott through a number of low wage jobs: fact...

verdict.reason: Chris Smith's debut has genuine observational power about wage-work exhaustion, but the 95-minute runtime and thin narrative structure work better on a smaller screen. Metrograph's DCP presentation is clean, though the film doesn't demand theatrical scale.

movies.title: A Better Tomorrow III: Love and Death in Saigon

ratings.plot: A man travels from China to Vietnam, on the brink of war with America, to retrieve his uncle and cousin but find complications when he falls in love with a female gangster with a dangerous ex.

verdict.reason: Hark Tsui's Vietnam-set action film has the visual flair and genre energy that makes his work worth catching, but the narrative sprawl and tonal shifts test patience over two hours. Metrograph's DCP restoration shows off the neon-soaked cinematography and fight choreography that justifies the theatrical setting.

movies.title: Ghost in the Shell: 30th Anniversary Remaster

ratings.plot: A young boy witnesses his mother's cheating ways and, after the death of his sick father, grows to despise her. When he's adopted by another family, the road to reconciliation proves achingly difficult.

verdict.reason: A rare 1973 Taiwanese family drama worth seeing if you're open to slow-burn emotional work, but the restoration at Metrograph is the only reason to catch it theatrically rather than wait for home viewing. The DCP print brings clarity to a film that has sat in obscurity for decades.

movies.title: This Long Century Presents: Salomé Lamas

ratings.plot: Ten years have passed since our three heroines' first outing in 1975. Now the women meet at yet another class reunion. Not surprisingly, they are still unwilling to call it a night after the party is over. Husbands and children mu...

verdict.reason: A sequel to Breien's 1975 film that works best if you've seen the original, but the DCP restoration at Metrograph makes it worth catching up on if Nordic comedy-drama about women's lives interests you. The 88-minute runtime is forgiving, and Breien's approach to female friendship and domestic life has aged better than most '80s fare.

ratings.plot: A successful Crown Court Judge's personal life as karaoke lover, wife and mom is shaken when a crisis hits. Can she keep her family stable while managing her career?

verdict.reason: Skip the subway if you need a knockout evening, but the 120-minute runtime and intimate character study make it solid homework on a quiet night. This is stage work on a screen—powerful if you're in the mood for theater, disposable if you want cinema.

movies.title: 2026 Sundance Film Festival Short Film Tour

ratings.plot: Documents the romantic journey of PK Mahanandia, a Delhi street artist who trekked 6,000 miles by bicycle in 1977, venturing across continents to reunite with the woman he loved.

verdict.reason: A real love story across continents has genuine pull, but the film depends on whether you want to sit with a personal documentary or need more formal theatrical ambition. Orlando von Einsiedel has made strong work before, and a 98-minute runtime keeps the premise from wearing out its welcome.

ratings.plot: Teen Isabel's attraction to Dr. Palanca at her country club job turns dark as she uncovers violence beneath the club's facade and discovers their disturbing connection from the past.

verdict.reason: Rafael Manuel's film has genuine unsettling power, but the runtime and tonal shifts demand patience on a big screen rather than at home. Film Forum's single-theater run means the screening window is narrow and the audience self-selected.

movies.title: MARIO PUZO’S THE GODFATHER, CODA: THE DEATH OF MICHAEL CORLEONE

ratings.plot: Former competitive runner turned photographer Aisha McAdams documents elite ultra marathon athletes. After trauma forced her from the sport, she wonders if she can find her way back by entering an ultra-marathon herself.

verdict.reason: A debut documentary about endurance sport and personal recovery has genuine stakes, but 102 minutes is a long runtime for a niche subject that works better as a intimate character study than a theatrical event. Max Lowe's previous work shows promise, yet this feels more suited to streaming or a festival circuit than a weeknight multiplex trip.

ratings.plot: When a rogue squad of genetically engineered super soldiers break loose in the desert, a badass Army sniper must unleash hell to protect her young daughter.

verdict.reason: Adam Wingard knows how to stage action with real kinetic force, but a 92-minute genre picture needs to justify the theater trip on execution alone. Catch it in 4DX if you want the spectacle to earn its seat price; otherwise, streaming will do the job.

movies.title: Star Trek: The Motion Picture – The Director's Edition + Season 2 Episode 3: 'The Changeling'

ratings.plot: A man takes his sick mother and nine family members on a single-day temple pilgrimage after his boss predicts she may die soon.

verdict.reason: A debut feature from a Thai filmmaker working in an intimate mode—worth seeing if you trust Lincoln Center's curatorial judgment on emerging international voices. The single-day structure and family ensemble suggest a quiet, character-driven film that may play better on a second viewing at home.

movies.title: A Day in the Life of Jo

ratings.plot: As a patronizing sister takes her estranged brother for a walk, she tries to explore his motivation about joining the Armed Forces of Ukraine.

verdict.reason: A short film about difficult family reconciliation during wartime has real substance, but its impact depends on your tolerance for interpersonal tension and whether you can catch it at Lincoln Center before it cycles out. The walk-and-talk format lives or dies on the performances and the specificity of what the sister actually learns.

ratings.plot: 'Please Have Me Executed.' Those were the first words spoken on a miserable, rainy day by a man arrested under suspicion of murdering his wife and son. His wish was to reunite with his wife and son as soon as he could. The veteran...

verdict.reason: A rare screening of an obscure Japanese drama about confession and justice that deserves attention for its formal restraint and moral complexity. The 90-minute runtime and single-venue run at Lincoln Center make this a now-or-never choice for those drawn to austere procedural cinema.

ratings.plot: A young theatre director Petr Dresler accepts an offer to direct the show "Last Train to Sussex Has Gone" in a great Prague theatre. The play is a modern piece of art from a famous author ...

verdict.reason: A Czech backstage comedy about theatrical ambition has real charm, but it's a minor regional film playing a single venue with no restoration or special occasion attached. Watch it if you're at Lincoln Center for something else and have time to kill; otherwise, this one doesn't justify the trip.

ratings.plot: Classical Period is a portrait of Cal and his friends in Philadelphia. They meet and have long conversations about books, poetry, music, and architecture, most notably Henry Longfellow's 1864 translation of Dante's Divine Comedy ....

verdict.reason: A 62-minute film of conversation about books and poetry has genuine charm, but it asks a lot of patience for modest rewards. Fendt's quiet naturalism works best on a smaller screen where you control the pacing.

ratings.plot: N/A

verdict.reason: A three-hour opera film demands commitment, but Metge's take on Mozart's comedy has real wit if you're in the mood for theatrical excess. The Lincoln Center screening gives you the proper scale, though streaming at home won't punish you much.

verdict.reason: A 1988 drama with minimal metadata makes this a blind commitment, but Film at Lincoln Center's selection suggests repertory merit worth investigating if you trust their curation. Check the program notes before buying your ticket.

movies.title: I Deserve a Lover Whose Every
In Which Annie Gives It Those

ratings.plot: Annie struggles to to clear his bachelor's degree with one final hurdle-The Thesis. It's his final attempt to clear it. Can he?

verdict.reason: A rare 1989 Indian comedy from Pradip Krishen deserves the Lincoln Center screening, but the thin premise and two-hour runtime demand patience if you're unfamiliar with the film's reputation. The theatrical venue and print quality justify a trip only if you're hunting for overlooked work from this era and director.

verdict.reason: A 1912 Italian film at Lincoln Center is historically significant but requires patience with silent-era pacing and image degradation. See it if you are committed to early cinema archaeology; skip it if you need theatrical polish.

verdict.reason: Skip it unless you're committed to three hours of Puccini opera in a theatrical setting. The 1991 staging prioritizes sung drama over spectacle, which works best on a cinema screen with pristine sound.

ratings.plot: Richard Wagner's last opera has remained controversial since its first performance for its unique, and, for some, unsavory blending of religious and erotic themes and imagery. Based on one of the medieval epic romances of King Art...

verdict.reason: Syberberg's four-hour operatic vision is uncompromising and visually baroque, but demands absolute commitment and tolerance for his deliberately confrontational staging of Wagner's final work. The theatrical experience is singular, though patience and appetite for avant-garde opera aesthetics are prerequisites.

ratings.plot: The story revolves around the incidents following the death of a young Naxalite, upon whose death his friends travel to the village where his mother lives to inform her of the death of her only son.

verdict.reason: A rare screening of an obscure 1986 Indian political drama about grief and state violence—worth seeing if you seek out work beyond the festival circuit. Lincoln Center's archive programming makes this the only accessible way to experience John Abraham's direction on the subject of Naxalite resistance and maternal loss.

ratings.plot: While the rest of the Hebrews bewail their fate, Samson alone trusts in God's promise of liberty. Abimelech, the Philistine satrap of Gaza, enters to mock the Hebrews' God, proclaiming the superiority of Dagon, and the Hebrews are...

verdict.reason: A filmed opera from a 1981 production—worthwhile if you want grand vocal performance on a big screen, but the two-hour runtime and static staging make this better suited to home viewing with a pause button. Browning's direction prioritizes the singers over cinematic language, so you're essentially watching a stage performance captured in a theater.

ratings.plot: When blues musician Al Cook's memory-filled apartment faces demolition, an old dream emerges from his isolated life.

verdict.reason: A modest character study with genuine emotional weight, but the 86-minute runtime and narrow focus make it better suited to a quiet night at home. Lincoln Center's programming gives it theatrical legitimacy, yet the film doesn't demand a big screen to land.

movies.title: Amyl and The Sniffers Present Truth or Consequence

ratings.plot: Truth or Consequence is a live album following the concert film of the same title, in which Amyl and The Sniffers perform country-influenced versions of their songs, two unreleased tracks, and a cover of the Slim Dusty classic "Lights On The Hill." It was recorded and filmed in front of an intimate and increasingly rowdy audience at El Coyote in Los Angeles on April 28, 2025, by the band's long-time collaborator John Angus Stewart. Screens with Amyl and The Sniffers 2025 concert film LIVE AT ALLY PALLY, mixed in 5.1 Dolby surround sound.

verdict.reason: Skip it unless you're committed to the band's sound and willing to sit through 90 minutes of a live album recording. The intimate El Coyote show has energy, but a concert film paired with a live album is a niche experience that works better for devoted fans than casual viewers seeking theatrical value.

ratings.plot: A notorious mafia hitman and a young Black FBI agent team up to investigate the murders of civil rights leaders in 1966 Mississippi.

verdict.reason: Elegance Bratton's debut feature has an audacious premise, but a hitman-FBI agent buddy dynamic risks undercutting the weight of 1966 Mississippi and the real murders it's built on. The film's theatrical value hinges entirely on whether Bratton's direction can hold tension across two hours without sacrificing the historical stakes for genre convenience.

ratings.plot: Presented in Japanese with English subtitles Come and join Crunchyroll for an exclusive sneak peek at the new October season, before it hits streaming. We will be screening select episodes of new seasons for the first time. A can’t-miss theatrical event!

verdict.reason: Skip the hype if you're not invested in fall anime lineups; this is a promotional sampler, not a complete film. The appeal lives or dies on which shows Crunchyroll has picked and whether you care about seeing them weeks early on a big screen instead of at home.

movies.title: Practical Magic 2 Midnight Margarita Dress-Up Screening

ratings.plot: Twenty-seven years after Sally and Gillian Owens first bewitched us, Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman return with a new generation of family magic and an old curse threatening to unravel it all. The original gave us midnight margaritas, broom mishaps, and Gillian’s eternally enviable wardrobe. Now, the Owens family has another curse to deal with, plus a whole new generation of witches. Bring your whole coven to Alamo Drafthouse and see what kind of trouble the Owens sisters get into this time.

verdict.reason: A nostalgia-driven sequel with the original cast reunited, but 27 years is a long gap and sequels to beloved films rarely justify the wait. The dress-up screening at Alamo Drafthouse adds social energy, but that's a mood purchase, not a film quality one.

ratings.plot: A multi generational family of witches, cursed to be loveless for centuries, attempts to break the spell by confronting dark secrets and sacrificing for each other.

verdict.reason: Susanne Bier brings serious dramatic weight to a franchise sequel, but two hours and ten minutes testing whether a love curse payoff justifies the runtime is a commitment. The multigenerational structure works better on repeat viewing than first night discovery.

ratings.plot: After a seven-year hiatus following the devastating loss of their beloved bandmate Chester Bennington, Linkin Park's remaining members struggle to find their way forward. Their shared history and enduring friendship, combined with the fresh perspective of two new band members, spark a renewed creative energy that leads them on a transformative journey of artistic reinvention. Following the band from intimate 2022 studio sessions through their explosive From Zero album release and concert in São Paulo, the film UNSHATTER weaves together rare vault footage, electrifying performances from sold-out shows, and candid interviews with band members and fans – capturing the raw, honest story of what it means to start over.

verdict.reason: Skip the theatrical run unless you need the crowd energy; this is a band documentary that works fine on a screen at home. The 107-minute runtime and concert footage don't demand a theater seat the way a live performance does.

movies.title: The Twilight Saga: New Moon Fan Screening

ratings.plot: The supernatural tale of star-crossed lovers continues as the Cullen family flees Forks in order to protect Bella (Kristen Stewart), and the heartbroken high-school senior discovers that vampires aren't the only creatures in town. Realizing that Bella will never be safe as long as he's around, Edward (Robert Pattinson) makes the difficult decision to leave his beloved behind shortly after her 18th birthday. Reeling from her loss, Bella embraces self-destruction after being comforted by Edward's image during a moment of mortal peril. But as heavy-hearted as Bella may be, her friend Jacob (Taylor Lautner) distracts her from her sorrows by helping her renovate a weather-beaten motorbike. When Bella encounters a former adversary with a sizable grudge, she's rescued from harm at the last second by a pack of enormous, ferocious wolves. Subsequently delving into the history of the Quileutes, Bella discovers the secrets of Jacob's tribe while looking forward to a reunion with Edward that may have deadly consequences.

verdict.reason: Skip the theatrical trip unless you're committed to the communal fan experience at Alamo Drafthouse. The film itself plays better at home, and a 131-minute runtime demands comfort you won't find in a movie theater seat.

ratings.plot: TWILIGHT is an action-packed, modern-day love story between a teen girl and a vampire. Bella Swan (Kristen Stewart) has always been a bit different, never fitting in with the girls at her school. When Bella is sent to live with her father in the rainy little town of Forks, Washington, she doesn’t expect much to change. Then she meets the mysterious and dazzlingly beautiful Edward Cullen (Robert Pattinson), a boy unlike any she’s ever met. Edward is a vampire, but he doesn’t have fangs and his family is unique in that they choose not to drink human blood. Edward has been waiting 90 years for a soul mate, which he finds in Bella. They are soon swept up in a passionate and unorthodox romance. Edward must struggle to resist the primal pull of her scent, which could send him into an uncontrollable frenzy, but what will they do when a clan of new vampires – James (Cam Gigandet), Laurent (Edi Gathegi), and Victoria (Rachelle Lefevre) – come to town and threaten to disrupt their way of life?

verdict.reason: Skip the theatrical trip unless you're in the mood for nostalgic communal viewing with fellow fans. The Alamo Drafthouse screenings trade theatrical immersion for crowd energy, which is the only reason to leave home for a film better experienced alone or streaming.

ratings.plot: In plague-ravaged 14th century England a peasant triggers a rebellion against King Richard II and unintentionally becomes a legend of resistance.

verdict.reason: Greengrass brings kinetic energy to a medieval uprising, but 128 minutes of his signature shaky-cam approach to 14th-century peasant revolt may test your tolerance for motion and noise over stillness. Worth it if you want propulsive action cinema; skip if you prefer restraint in historical drama.

ratings.plot: Widowed pear salesman Ernie Tyler travels to scatter his wife's ashes in places she specified, each location stirring memories that help him process their marriage, his work life, and his future.

verdict.reason: A modest indie comedy about grief that works best if you connect with Bruce Campbell's understated direction and the intimate pacing of a 90-minute road movie. The Alamo Drafthouse venues are solid but not a draw—this film has no theatrical urgency and plays just fine at home later.

movies.title: Breaking Bad Day Free TV Party Screening

ratings.plot: September 7 is Breaking Bad Day, so we're celebrating the only way that makes sense: with a one-night-only interactive screening of Breaking Bad 's legendary Season 4 finale, "Face Off." Admission is free with the purchase of a fully redeemable and refundable $10 food and beverage voucher. Join a live host in a yellow hazmat suit and collect your themed keepsakes: Hector Salamanca's bell, a Heisenberg hat, blue rock candy, and a Gus Fring half-face mask. Then get ready to experience one of television's greatest episodes with a theater full of fellow fans. Reserve your spot now. Let’s cook.

verdict.reason: Free admission and themed merch make this a fun night out, but a 75-minute TV episode on a theater screen is not a theatrical experience—it's a fan gathering that happens to use a projector. Go if you want the crowd and the props; skip if you want cinema.

movies.title: Pulp: What Do You Do for an Encore?

ratings.plot: Charting the Sheffield band’s extraordinary journey from obscurity to cultural touchstone. Fusing footage from Pulp’s biggest ever arena show – part of the global tour for ‘More’, the band’s first album in 24 years – with four decades of colourful, never-seen-before archival material.

verdict.reason: Essential for Pulp devotees, but a 99-minute concert doc plays better at home than in a theater built for food and chatter. The archival material is the real draw—unseen footage from four decades justifies the trip only if you're committed to the band's full story.

ratings.plot: Imagine that a local cable station was invaded by otherdimensional creatures at the stroke of midnight. That's Video Vortex. Each month, this series presents a mystery transmission that's culled from the outer limits of home video history – from essential underground films to surreal docs, from tokusatsu battle-parties to outsider experiments. So warm up the cathode tubes, dim the lights, and let your senses intermingle with the glow.

verdict.reason: Skip it unless you're already committed to the Video Vortex series or have a taste for deep-cut oddities from home video history. At 77 minutes, it's a low-stakes gamble, but the appeal depends entirely on what this month's transmission actually contains.

ratings.plot: A sexy temptress no man can resist and a local police officer who falls hard for her become embroiled in a complicated intrigue of passion and jealousy in Radley Metzger's boldly original erotic update of the opera Carmen.

verdict.reason: Skip the hype around the premise and commit only if you're interested in Metzger's formal style in 1967 erotic cinema. The 87-minute runtime is mercifully brief, but this is a footnote in his career, not essential viewing.

ratings.plot: A night of attempted seduction is recalled from the perspectives of the woman, the man, a lecherous doorman and a psychoanalyst.

verdict.reason: Bava's playful take on unreliable narration has charm, but the film is a minor entry in his catalog that works better as a curiosity than a necessary theatrical event. The 83-minute runtime and lightweight premise suit a home viewing just as well, unless you're committed to seeing Bava's full range on the big screen.
